summary:
What if anyone could explore the sky and see what has changed over time?

SLOWTRACE X is an interactive web platform that makes real observations from NASA's SPHEREx telescope accessible to everyone. Users can choose a location in the sky, retrieve infrared images from different dates, and compare them to look for changes and possible moving objects.

We developed an observation viewer, an interactive 3D sky atlas, a Solar System explorer, scientific visualizations, and DeepTrace, an experimental tool that searches for faint motion across multiple observations.

We also built an automated survey pipeline that has processed 500 unique SPHEREx detector images, with recorded results that can be inspected and verified. Our current candidates are preliminary findings, not confirmed discoveries.

SLOWTRACE X brings real astronomical data and scientific investigation into one accessible experience. Our goal is to make exploring the changing universe easier, more engaging, and more transparent for students, researchers, and curious minds everywhere.
details:
The Idea Behind SLOWTRACE X

The universe is constantly changing, but noticing those changes is not always easy. Stars move, objects change in brightness, and faint signals can be hidden within enormous amounts of astronomical data.

NASA's SPHEREx mission observes the sky in 102 infrared bands. These observations give us an opportunity to study the universe in ways that visible-light images alone cannot.

For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we wanted to build something that would make this data easier to explore while also giving users tools to investigate what they find.

That is how SLOWTRACE X began.

How Our Project Works

SLOWTRACE X is a public web application that allows users to explore real NASA SPHEREx observations.

A user can enter astronomical coordinates or choose a featured target. The platform searches NASA's Infrared Science Archive for available observations and loads actual telescope data from different dates.

Our observation viewer aligns the available images so users can blink between them, compare observations, and inspect differences. Users can also explore wavelength information and view the original data sources.

We developed an interactive celestial globe and sky atlas to make navigating the sky more intuitive. The platform also includes a 3D Solar System explorer, scientific statistics, and research tools.

DeepTrace and Moving Object Investigation

One of our main additions is DeepTrace, an experimental motion detection system.

Instead of relying on a single image, DeepTrace examines compatible observations taken at different times and tests possible patterns of movement. It uses an established technique called shift and stack to investigate faint signals that might otherwise be difficult to identify.

Potential detections can then be examined alongside the original images and compared with information from astronomical catalogs such as Gaia DR3 and NASA JPL.

We do not treat every detected signal as a new object. Image artifacts, background sources, and measurement uncertainty can create misleading results. Our system is designed to make those uncertainties visible.

Our Automated Survey

We also developed an automated pipeline capable of processing larger collections of SPHEREx data.

During our initial verified run, the pipeline processed 500 unique NASA detector images and recorded their processing history. The resulting dataset includes 11 regions analyzed for motion and 200 preliminary review peaks.

These peaks remain unresolved and are not confirmed astronomical discoveries.

The system records image provenance, processing results, and interruptions so the work can be checked and resumed. Our long-term goal is to expand this approach toward a much larger survey.

Testing and Scientific Reliability

We wanted to demonstrate not only what our software can do, but also how its results should be evaluated.

Our Experiment Lab allows users to test known simulated signals against real SPHEREx image backgrounds.

In one recorded experiment involving eight injected sources, DeepTrace recovered two, while the best individual exposure also recovered two. This is an early result, not proof that our method outperforms other approaches.

Being transparent about limitations is an important part of our project.

Technology and Development

We built SLOWTRACE X using React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, Three.js, and other open-source development tools.

NASA's SPHEREx archive supplies the astronomical observations. Gaia and JPL resources help provide scientific context and support candidate investigations.

The platform uses interactive 3D visualizations, scientific charts, image comparison tools, and a persistent processing system. The website is deployed through Vercel, with source code and documentation available on GitHub.

AI-assisted development helped us research, write, test, and improve parts of the application. The astronomical observations are authentic NASA data, and simulated experimental signals are clearly identified.

What Makes SLOWTRACE X Different

Our approach is to bring several parts of astronomical investigation together in one place.

Users can move from exploring the sky to opening telescope observations, comparing images, investigating a possible signal, and reviewing the supporting evidence.

Rather than simply displaying astronomical images, we want to make the process of scientific discovery accessible and understandable.

SLOWTRACE X is designed for students, astronomy enthusiasts, educators, citizen scientists, and anyone curious about the universe.

We have not discovered Planet X or confirmed a new astronomical object. What we have created is a working platform that helps people ask better questions using real NASA data.

We believe that exploring the universe should not be limited to those who already know how to work with complex astronomical archives.

Sometimes, discovering something new begins with simply knowing where to look.

The complete source code, scientific methodology, processing scripts, validation results, and documentation are publicly available on GitHub.
